title: Supreme Court Says California Can Keep Counting Its Ballots
summary:
The United States Supreme Court has said no to a last-minute request to change how California counts votes in the midterm elections.

The midterm elections decide which political party controls Congress for the last two years of President Donald Trump's second term. Voting ends on Tuesday, November 3.

The Justice Department had asked the court to set aside 20,000 ballots. It said those ballots may have been issued to people who are not United States citizens. On Monday, the court answered with a one-line order denying the request. Lower-court rulings will stand, and the effort to disqualify those ballots has essentially ended.

California is the most populous state, with about 23 million people on its voting register. By Sunday night, more than six million mail-in ballots had been received, according to the California secretary of state's office.

Last month, the Justice Department sent letters to California's secretary of state and to Los Angeles County's registrar, asking them to separate the 20,000 ballots. On Friday, a federal appeals court declined that request, amid concern that eligible voters could lose their votes and that separating ballots while voting is underway is not workable.

The request was part of a years-long campaign by Trump and his administration against what they describe as widespread voter fraud, even though research has found such fraud to be extremely rare. Trump has repeatedly claimed that Democrats steal elections by allowing immigrants to vote illegally, and he has blamed mail-in voting, which is permitted in many states.

Last week, district judge David Carter described the government's move in California as an "ongoing pattern of attempted election interference." He said that never before in American history had the federal government, on the eve of an election, tried to press a state and local government to abandon their own election procedures.
why_it_matters: The ruling decides whether thousands of California ballots stay in the count, and it shows how courts can protect eligible voters' ballots during an election.

options: A request to move the election date
A request to set aside 20,000 California ballots
A request to count all California votes twice
A request to close California polls early

Because they were damaged by rain

background_read: In the United States, voters choose members of Congress in midterm elections, which happen in the middle of a president's term.
Mail-in ballots are votes sent by post instead of cast in person at a polling place.
Courts can be asked to set aside ballots, but judges weigh whether that would unfairly stop eligible voters from having their votes counted.
The Supreme Court is the highest court in the United States, and its decisions stand above those of lower courts.
